Acronyms 97

ACR-F
Attenuation to Crosstalk Ratio, Far End. How much stronger the signal is than the far-end crosstalk noise.
AHJ
Authority Having Jurisdiction. The inspector, fire marshal, or building official whose decision on a code question is final.
AP
Access Point. The wireless radio unit that connects devices to the cabled network, usually through PoE.
APC
Angled Physical Contact. A fiber connector with an angled end face; the body is green.
AWG
American Wire Gauge. The conductor size scale: the lower the number, the thicker the wire.
BAS
Building Automation System. The controls that run heating, cooling, lighting, and other building services.
BCT
Bonding Conductor for Telecommunications. The conductor that joins the PBB to the building's grounding electrode.
BICSI
Building Industry Consulting Service International. The association that runs the Installer 1, Installer 2, Technician, and RCDD credentials.
BNC
Bayonet Neill-Concelman. A twist-lock coax connector used on security video and test equipment.
CATV
Community Antenna Television. The general-purpose listing for coax and cable television cable.
CATVP
Community Antenna Television, Plenum. The plenum listing for coax cable.
CATVR
Community Antenna Television, Riser. The riser listing for coax cable.
CM
Communications, general. The general-purpose communications cable listing: no plenum or riser use.
CMG
Communications, general purpose. The general-purpose communications cable listing, equal to CM.
CMP
Communications, plenum. The plenum communications cable listing: the highest rating, allowed in air-handling spaces.
CMR
Communications, riser. The riser communications cable listing: for vertical runs through a firestopped opening.
CMX
Communications, limited use. The limited-use communications cable listing: dwellings and raceways, short runs.
DAS
Distributed Antenna System. A set of antennas that spreads cellular or public safety radio coverage through a building.
EF
Entrance Facility. Where outside cabling enters the building, with the protectors and the primary bonding busbar.
EMI
Electromagnetic Interference. Electrical noise from power wiring, motors, and lamps that can corrupt cable signals.
EMT
Electrical Metallic Tubing. Thin-wall steel conduit; a common pathway for horizontal cable.
ENT
Electrical Nonmetallic Tubing. Flexible corrugated plastic conduit, used in some walls and slabs.
ER
Equipment Room. The room for equipment that serves the whole building or campus.
FEXT
Far-End Crosstalk. Signal that leaks from one pair into another at the far end of the link.
FTP
Foiled Twisted Pair. Twisted-pair cable with a foil shield; the F in F/UTP and S/FTP stands for foil.
HC
Horizontal Cross-connect. The point on a floor where horizontal cabling is connected to patch panels and equipment.
HDTDR
High-Definition Time-Domain Reflectometry. A tester display that shows where along a link a reflection (return loss problem) occurs.
HDTDX
High-Definition Time-Domain Crosstalk. A tester display that shows where along a link crosstalk is coming from.
HVAC
Heating, Ventilating, and Air Conditioning. The building systems that move and condition air, including the ducts and plenums above the ceiling.
IC
Intermediate Cross-connect. The optional middle level of the backbone, between the main and horizontal cross-connects.
ICT
Information and Communications Technology. The trades that install and maintain cabling and the systems that ride on it.
ID
Inside Diameter. The measure across the inside of a conduit; fill is calculated from it.
IDC
Insulation Displacement Connector. A jaw that cuts through wire insulation as the conductor is punched down.
IEC
International Electrotechnical Commission. The international body for electrical and electronic standards, a partner of ISO.
IL
Insertion Loss. The signal lost along the link; lower is better.
IN101
Installation 101. The BICSI class that prepares a candidate for the Installer 1 hands-on and written exams.
INST1
Installer 1. BICSI's entry-level installation certificate: a six-task hands-on exam, then a 75-question written exam.
INSTC
Installer 2 Copper. The next BICSI installation certificate after Installer 1, focused on copper cabling.
INSTF
Installer 2 Optical Fiber. The next BICSI installation certificate after Installer 1, focused on optical fiber cabling.
ISO
International Organization for Standardization. The international body that, with the IEC, publishes the ISO/IEC 11801 cabling standard.
ITS
Information Transport System. The cabling and pathways that carry signals through a building or campus.
LC
Lucent Connector. A small form factor fiber connector with a latch, common on new work.
LED
Light-Emitting Diode. The common light source for multimode fiber links.
MC
Main Cross-connect. The top of the backbone hierarchy, usually in the equipment room.
MHz
Megahertz. The unit for the frequency a cable category is rated to carry.
MPO
Multi-fiber Push On. A connector that carries many fibers in one ferrule, used for high-density links.
NEC
National Electrical Code. The model electrical code, published by NFPA as NFPA 70 and adopted into law by each jurisdiction.
NEXT
Near-End Crosstalk. Signal that leaks from one pair into another at the near end of the link.
NFPA
National Fire Protection Association. The group that writes the NEC (NFPA 70) and the fire alarm code (NFPA 72).
NRTL
Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory. A lab approved to test products and list them for a stated use.
NVP
Nominal Velocity of Propagation. The speed of signal in the cable as a percent of the speed of light, used to compute length.
OD
Outside Diameter. The measure across the outside of a cable; bend radius and conduit fill are calculated from it.
OFCP
Optical Fiber, Conductive, Plenum. A plenum listing for fiber that has metal strength members or armor.
OFCR
Optical Fiber, Conductive, Riser. A riser listing for fiber that has metal strength members or armor.
OFN
Optical Fiber, Nonconductive. A general-purpose listing for fiber with no metal parts.
OFNP
Optical Fiber, Nonconductive, Plenum. A plenum listing for fiber with no metal parts.
OFNR
Optical Fiber, Nonconductive, Riser. A riser listing for fiber with no metal parts.
OLTS
Optical Loss Test Set. A light source and power meter used to measure total fiber link loss.
OM1
Optical Multimode 1. A 62.5 micron multimode fiber grade, with an orange jacket.
OM2
Optical Multimode 2. A 50 micron multimode fiber grade, with an orange jacket.
OM3
Optical Multimode 3. A laser-optimized 50 micron multimode grade, with an aqua jacket.
OM4
Optical Multimode 4. A higher-bandwidth laser-optimized 50 micron multimode grade, with an aqua jacket.
OM5
Optical Multimode 5. A wideband 50 micron multimode grade, with a lime green jacket.
OS1
Optical Singlemode 1. A singlemode fiber grade for indoor use, with a yellow jacket.
OS2
Optical Singlemode 2. A singlemode fiber grade for outdoor and long-distance use, with a yellow jacket.
OSHA
Occupational Safety and Health Administration. The federal agency whose rules govern jobsite safety, PPE, ladders, and hazard communication.
OTDR
Optical Time-Domain Reflectometer. A tester that shows where loss and reflections occur along a fiber.
PBB
Primary Bonding Busbar. The main busbar for telecommunications bonding, one per building, formerly called the TMGB.
PD
Powered Device. The camera, phone, or access point that receives PoE power.
PoE
Power over Ethernet. Power delivered over the same twisted pairs that carry data.
PPE
Personal Protective Equipment. Safety glasses, gloves, hard hat, shoes, and other gear that protects the worker.
PSE
Power Sourcing Equipment. The switch or injector that supplies PoE power.
PSNEXT
Power Sum Near-End Crosstalk. The combined crosstalk that the other three pairs put on one pair.
PVC
Polyvinyl Chloride. Rigid plastic conduit, commonly used underground or in slabs.
RCDD
Registered Communications Distribution Designer. A BICSI design credential, several steps above the installer certificates.
RFI
Radio-Frequency Interference. Noise from radio transmitters and similar sources that couples into cabling.
RG
Radio Guide. The prefix for a family of coax types such as RG-6, RG-59, and RG-11.
RL
Return Loss. Signal reflected back by impedance mismatches, often from a poor termination.
SBB
Secondary Bonding Busbar. A busbar in a telecommunications room or equipment room, formerly called the TGB.
SC
Subscriber Connector. A square push-pull fiber connector, common on patch panels.
SCS
Structured Cabling System. A planned, standards-based set of cabling subsystems that serves many applications.
ST
Straight Tip. A round bayonet fiber connector with a twist lock, from an older generation.
STP
Shielded Twisted Pair. A general name for twisted-pair cable with a shield around the pairs, the cable, or both.
T568A
TIA-568 wiring scheme A. One of two standard 8-pin color orders: pin 1 is white-green.
T568B
TIA-568 wiring scheme B. One of two standard 8-pin color orders: pin 1 is white-orange.
TBB
Telecommunications Bonding Backbone. The insulated copper conductor that ties the PBB to the SBBs between floors.
TE
Telecommunications Enclosure. A cabinet that serves a small area on a floor, never a replacement for a telecommunications room.
TEBC
Telecommunications Equipment Bonding Conductor. The older name for the rack bonding conductor, 6 AWG minimum, green, from busbar to rack.
TGB
Telecommunications Grounding Busbar. The older name for the secondary bonding busbar (SBB).
TIA
Telecommunications Industry Association. The standards body that writes the TIA-568, 569, 606, and 607 documents.
TMGB
Telecommunications Main Grounding Busbar. The older name for the primary bonding busbar (PBB).
TR
Telecommunications Room. The room on each floor where horizontal cabling ends on patch panels.
UL
Underwriters Laboratories. A nationally recognized testing laboratory that lists cable, firestop systems, and hardware.
UPC
Ultra Physical Contact. A fiber connector with a polished flat end face; the body is blue.
UTP
Unshielded Twisted Pair. Twisted-pair copper cable with no shield; the most common horizontal cable.
VCSEL
Vertical-Cavity Surface-Emitting Laser. A low-cost laser used with laser-optimized multimode fiber.
WA
Work Area. The space where people use the system: the outlet, the patch cord, and the station equipment.

The exam itself 19

Credential
BICSI Installer 1 (INST1): the entry-level installation certificate for the ICT trades. It is nonrenewable
Two parts
A hands-on exam first, then the written exam. Both must be passed. The written exam can only be taken after the hands-on is passed
Hands-on
Six tasks done to industry standards, 20 minutes per task. The proctor gives pass or fail after each task
Hands-on timing
Given on the last day of the IN101 class, generally Friday afternoon
Hands-on retest
One failed task may be retested the same day at no cost. Failing the same task twice, or failing two tasks, means retaking the hands-on on another date
Written exam
75 multiple-choice questions testing knowledge and application, 2 hours, computer-based at a Pearson testing site
Tools at the written exam
A calculator and a whiteboard are provided. There are no scheduled breaks
Passing score
Set by a panel of experts using a standard-setting method. BICSI does not publish it. A failing candidate gets a score report by topic area, not a score
Experience required
None. Recommended: the IN101 class, about 50 hours of self-study, and safety and PPE training
Physical requirements
Tell colors apart, work with good manual dexterity, stand for long periods, climb ladders, and lift and carry up to 50 pounds
Application
At least seven days before the hands-on date
Exam fee
$335 for a BICSI member, $400 for a nonmember. It covers the first hands-on attempt and the first written attempt
Retest fee
$135 member, $200 nonmember
Virtual walk-in hands-on
$135
Waiting periods
30 days between unsuccessful attempts; 90 days after a third unsuccessful attempt
Eligibility window
One year from your first hands-on attempt
Identification
A government photo ID with your signature plus a secondary ID. The name must match your BICSI profile
Next steps
Installer 2 Copper (INSTC) and Installer 2 Optical Fiber (INSTF). The design path later leads to the RCDD
How the questions read
Jobsite scenarios that ask for the FIRST step, the MOST likely cause, or the BEST method or material

The cabling system 16

Work area (WA)
Where people use the system: the outlet, the patch cord, and the equipment on the desk. Two outlets minimum per work area
Horizontal cabling (HC)
The cable from the outlet in the work area back to the patch panel in the telecom room on the same floor
Telecommunications room (TR)
Serves one floor or part of one. Holds patch panels, racks, switches, and the cross-connects for horizontal and backbone cabling
Telecommunications enclosure (TE)
A cabinet that serves a small space on a floor. It is never a substitute for a TR
Backbone cabling
The cable between TRs, equipment rooms, and entrance facilities. Cabling between two TRs is backbone, even on one floor
Equipment room (ER)
Serves the whole building or campus. Houses large common equipment and terminates backbone cabling. It can also serve as an entrance facility
Entrance facility (EF)
Where outside cabling enters the building. Holds the protectors, the demarcation, and the primary bonding busbar
Structured cabling system (SCS)
The whole planned system of subsystems above, built to one standard. A building's information transport system (ITS) is the same idea
Main cross-connect (MC)
The top of the backbone hierarchy, usually in the equipment room
Intermediate cross-connect (IC)
The optional middle level between the main cross-connect and a floor's horizontal cross-connect
Horizontal cross-connect
Where horizontal cabling meets the patch panel and equipment, normally in the TR
Telecommunications outlet
The wall or furniture jack that ends the horizontal cable, in the work area
Shape
A hierarchical star: every floor reaches back to a higher level, never in a ring or a chain
Cross-connects in the horizontal
One level only. No tandem patch panels between the outlet and the TR
Cross-connects in the backbone
At most two levels: the main and one intermediate
Bridged taps and splices
Not allowed in horizontal copper cabling

Copper, fiber, and coax 21

UTP
Unshielded twisted pair: the most common horizontal cable
F/UTP
Foil over the whole cable, no shield on the individual pairs
STP
Shielded twisted pair: a general name for cable with a shield around the pairs or the whole cable
S/FTP
Braid over the cable and foil on each pair; the shield must be bonded
23 AWG and 24 AWG
Conductor sizes; the lower the number, the thicker the wire. Category 6A is often 23 AWG
Solid conductor
Used for permanent horizontal runs and punched down on an insulation displacement connector
Stranded conductor
Used for patch cords; it flexes without breaking but loses more signal, so cords stay short
Multipair
Bundled pairs for backbone voice cable, in 25-pair binder groups
Color-coded binder
A colored ribbon or thread that groups every 25 pairs inside a large multipair cable
Cladding diameter
125 micron for both multimode and singlemode
Tight buffer
A 900 micron coating on each fiber. Used inside buildings, easier to terminate, less water-resistant
Loose tube
Coated fibers with a 250 micron coating floating in a gel or dry tube. Used outdoors, must be transitioned inside the building
Multimode light source
LED or VCSEL, at 850 nm and 1300 nm
Singlemode light source
Laser, at 1310 nm and 1550 nm
Jacket color is voluntary
The color is a convention, not a law. Read the print on the jacket for the real fiber type
RG-6
75 ohm. The standard for video and cable television runs; the best choice in new work
RG-59
75 ohm. Older and thinner, with more loss; short video runs and closed-circuit cameras
RG-11
75 ohm. Thick, low-loss; long runs and outdoor feeder cable
Video systems
75 ohm
Radio systems
50 ohm
Connectors
F connector for cable television; BNC for security video and test equipment

Codes, listings, and standards 31

Code
A rule adopted into law, enforced by an inspector. The NEC is a code once your jurisdiction adopts it
Standard
A consensus document that sets the technical method. It becomes enforceable when a code, a contract, or a specification calls for it
AHJ
Authority having jurisdiction: the inspector, fire marshal, or building official whose decision wins. Mounting heights and permit rules are the AHJ's call
NRTL
Nationally recognized testing laboratory, such as UL. It lists and labels products
Listed
A product that an NRTL has tested and put on a published list for a stated use
Specification versus drawing
When they disagree, ask the designer in writing before you build. Do not guess
CMP
Plenum: air-handling spaces. The highest rating for communications cable
CMR
Riser: vertical runs between floors, through a firestopped opening
CMG and CM
General purpose: horizontal runs on one floor, but not in plenums or risers
CMX
Limited use: dwellings and raceways only, in short runs
OFNP
Optical fiber, nonconductive, plenum
OFNR
Optical fiber, nonconductive, riser
OFN
Optical fiber, nonconductive, general purpose
OFCP
Optical fiber, conductive (it has metal in it), plenum
OFCR
Optical fiber, conductive, riser
CATVP
Community antenna television and coax, plenum
CATVR
Coax, riser
CATV
Coax, general purpose
A higher rating can replace a lower one
A plenum cable may go where a riser or general cable is required; a riser cable may go where a general cable is required
A lower rating can never replace a higher one
General cable in a plenum or a riser is a violation, even for a short run
Order from highest to lowest
Plenum (P), then riser (R), then general (G or none), then limited (X)
Cable type must match its space
The jacket print tells you the rating. If the print is missing, treat the cable as unrated
TIA-568
The cabling standard: topology, distances, performance, connectors, and test methods
TIA-569
Pathways and spaces: rooms, trays, conduit, and boxes
TIA-606
Administration: labeling and records
TIA-607
Bonding and grounding for telecommunications
TIA-758
Outside plant, at recognition level only
ISO/IEC 11801
The international structured cabling standard, with its own class names
NFPA 70
The National Electrical Code (NEC): wiring, cable listings, bonding, and firestop of penetrations
NFPA 72
Fire alarm and signaling, at recognition level. Fire alarm work is separate from structured cabling
OSHA
The federal safety rules for your jobsite: PPE, ladders, trenching, hazard communication

Telecom spaces and bonding 41

Telecommunications room (TR)
At least one per floor. Placed so that no horizontal run passes 90 m. Horizontal cabling ends in a TR on the same floor
Equipment room (ER)
Serves the building or campus. Houses large equipment and terminates backbone and horizontal cabling
Entrance facility (EF)
Where public and private service cabling enters the building. Includes the entrance point at the building wall
Telecommunications enclosure (TE)
Serves at most 335 square meters (3600 square feet) on a floor. It does not replace a TR
Environment
Conditioned air, clean and dry, lit well enough to read a label, with power and bonding already in place
Do not put in a TR
Water pipes or drains over the equipment, unrelated equipment, storage, and anything that blocks the door
Door and access
Lockable, wide enough to move equipment, and clear of obstructions
Work and aisle space
If no distance is specified, plan at least 1 m (3.28 ft) around and between equipment
Material
Plywood, void free, A grade on the exposed side and C on the wall side, 15 percent moisture or less
Thickness
19 mm (3/4 in), recommended; sheets are 1.2 m by 2.4 m (4 ft by 8 ft)
Mounting height
From 203 mm (8 in) above the finished floor up to 2.6 m (8.5 ft). Do not split the difference in a taller room
Fire protection
Two coats of fire-retardant paint. If the code requires fire-retardant treated plywood, do not paint it; ask the AHJ whether to leave the stamp showing
Where
On at least two walls of a TR; all four if possible. Mount a 305 mm (12 in) tray on the same walls
Fasteners on studs
Align the sheet to the studs. On metal studs, screws at least 12.7 mm (0.5 in) longer than the plywood is thick
Fasteners in a hollow wall
Toggle bolts at least 6.3 mm (0.25 in) in diameter, 51 mm (2 in) from the edges, about every 610 mm (24 in)
Joints
No gaps between adjacent sheets
Width
483 mm (19 in) is the standard; 584 mm (23 in) racks are used by service providers
Height
2.1 m (7 ft) is the normal height
One rack unit
1 U is about 45 mm (1.75 in) of vertical space
Anchoring
Bolt a floor rack to the floor with expansion anchors, flat washers, and lock washers
Overhead support
Brace the top of the rack to the wall, a tray, or a ladder rack. Seismic bracing is whatever the AHJ requires
Access
Use double-sided racks and keep the front and the rear accessible
Equipment screws
M5, M6, 10-32, or 12-24 threads, with star washers for bonding
Wall-mounted rack
Lag bolts and washers into the plywood; check the wall will carry the full load
Cable management
Vertical managers at the sides, horizontal managers by each patch panel, and room for cord slack
D-rings
Fine for small bundles and cross-connect jumpers; never a replacement for a ladder rack
Primary bonding busbar (PBB)
Formerly the telecommunications main grounding busbar (TMGB). One per building, in the entrance facility, bonded straight to the service ground
Secondary bonding busbar (SBB)
Formerly the telecommunications grounding busbar (TGB). One or more per TR or ER, as many as needed
Telecommunications bonding backbone (TBB)
An insulated, stranded copper conductor from the PBB to each SBB, equalizing the floors
Bonding conductor for telecommunications (BCT)
Connects the PBB to the electrical service's grounding electrode system. Keep it as short as possible
Rack bonding conductor
Formerly the TEBC. 6 AWG minimum, stranded, insulated copper from the SBB or PBB to each rack and cabinet
Grounding equalizer
A 6 AWG minimum insulated copper conductor that evens out potentials between TRs
Jacket color
Green, or green with a yellow stripe, for every bonding conductor
Lugs
Two-hole compression lugs on every busbar and rack connection
Surface preparation
Scrape paint to bare metal, apply antioxidant compound, then make the connection
Daisy-chaining
Never. Each rack gets its own conductor back to the busbar
Busbar mounting
On insulated standoffs with at least 51 mm (2 in) of clearance behind it
Bend rules
Minimum bend radius of 203 mm (8 in); never a bend of less than 90 degrees
Bonding resistance
Two-point bonding test: 0.1 ohm (100 milliohms) is the recommended maximum
Conduits and trays
Metal conduit, tray, and ladder rack are bonded. A grounding bushing carries a 6 AWG copper wire to the busbar
Power cord ground
Never the only ground for a rack. The telecommunications ground path is separate and verifiable

Pathways 63

Fill, one cable
53 percent of the inside area
Fill, two cables
31 percent
Fill, three or more cables
40 percent
Bends between pull points
No more than two 90-degree bends
Distance between pull points
No more than 30 m (100 ft)
Bend radius, copper cable, trade size 2 in (53 mm) and smaller
6 x the inside diameter
Bend radius, copper cable, larger than 2 in
10 x the inside diameter
Bend radius, conduit carrying optical fiber
10 x the inside diameter
Conduit types
EMT is thin-wall steel tubing, ENT is flexible nonmetallic tubing, and PVC is rigid plastic. Each has its own inside diameter, so look it up before you calculate fill
Pull box
Add one where a run would otherwise exceed two bends or the pull length; it must stay accessible, never behind a finished wall
Conduit ends
Ream the cut ends and install bushings so the jacket is not cut
Pull string
Leave one in every empty conduit, and replace it whenever you pull
Sweeps
Use sweep elbows for fiber and large cables
Entering a TR
Conduit ends come in at the left side of the backboard. The interconnecting conduit is 78 mm (3 trade size) minimum, bushed and firestopped
1/2 in
0.622 in
3/4 in
0.824 in
1 in
1.049 in
1-1/4 in
1.380 in
1-1/2 in
1.610 in
2 in
2.067 in
Formula
Fill percent = number of cables x cable OD squared / conduit ID squared x 100
Worked example
Ten cables with a 0.25 in OD in 1 in EMT: 10 x 0.0625 / 1.1004 x 100 = 56.8 percent. That is over the 40 percent limit
Fix
At 40 percent, 1 in EMT carries 0.4 x 1.1004 / 0.0625 = 7 of those cables. Use a 1-1/4 in conduit or split the run
Use OD and ID
OD is the outside diameter of the cable; ID is the inside diameter of the conduit. Square each one
Round down
Always round the number of cables down, never up
Tubular ladder rack depth
38 mm (1.5 in); the width runs from 152 mm (6 in) to about 1 m (3.28 ft)
Threaded rod, heavy duty
16 mm (5/8 in) rod, properly anchored
Wire mesh tray supports
Within 0.6 m (2 ft) of each end and each side of a joint, then every 1.52 m (5 ft)
Rod-stock tray depths
51 mm (2 in), 100 mm (3.94 in), and 152 mm (6 in), usually in 3 m (10 ft) sections
Cutting a listed tray
Ask the AHJ first. A field cut can void the listing
Bonding
Every section is bonded, whether it carries power or low-voltage cable
Fill and depth
Set by the designer and the code. Use retaining posts so cable never rises above the side rails
Vertical runs
Secure each cable to the rung so the weight spreads over several supports
Riser core
A vertical ladder rack in a riser core passes through firestopped openings
Multiple levels
Firestopping between levels may be required
Maximum spacing
1.5 m (5 ft) apart
Sag
Even and shallow; the cable bundle must not rest on the ceiling or touch the tile grid
Attachment
Never to ceiling grid wires, to the grid itself, or to another trade's conduit, duct, or pipe
Independent support
Hang from the structure above with its own rod, strap, or beam clamp
Load
Do not exceed the hook's rated cable count; use bigger hooks or a tray
Fiber cords
Keep them off solid-bottom supports; use mesh, ladder, or noncontinuous supports to avoid pressure points
Branch circuits of 5 kVA or less
No extra separation needed
Unshielded power in open or nonmetal pathways
610 mm (24 in)
Unshielded power next to a grounded metal pathway
305 mm (12 in)
Power in grounded metal conduit next to a metal pathway
152 mm (6 in)
Electric motors and transformers
1220 mm (48 in)
Fluorescent, neon, mercury vapor, and discharge lamps
130 mm (5.12 in)
Arc welders
800 mm (31.5 in)
Induction heating equipment
1000 mm (39.37 in)
Single-gang and double-gang boxes
A box for one or two faceplates; deep enough for the cable bend radius
Cut-in ring or old-work bracket
Mounts a faceplate in existing drywall without a box
Low-voltage mounting bracket
Never in a fire or smoke barrier unless listed for it
Poke-through
A rated floor assembly installed to its listing; the cables in it must match the space below
Floor box
Fed through a floor core or a slab sleeve and firestopped to the listing
Furniture feed
A power pole or partition raceway; keep power and communications on separate sides
Mounting height
Set by the drawings and the AHJ; never guess it
Plenum boxes
A surface raceway in a plenum needs plenum-rated cable
Sleeve
A short pipe through a wall or floor. Bushed at both ends
Core
A round hole drilled through a floor or wall. Core where the drawings show; never into structure without approval
Slot
A rectangular floor opening for a riser. Frame it and firestop it
Spare capacity
Leave room for growth; do not fill a sleeve to its limit
Firestop
Every sleeve, core, and slot with cable through it gets a listed firestop system
Unused openings
Cap and label them, and firestop them too if the wall is rated

Firestopping 18

Firestop system
A listed system: a tested combination of materials and method for one specific penetration, in one specific wall or floor assembly
Why
To keep flame, heat, and smoke from passing through the opening and to restore the rating of the wall or floor
F rating
How many hours the system keeps flames from passing through. It also withstands a hose stream
T rating
How many hours the system keeps the temperature rise on the cold side below a limit
L rating
How well the system seals against smoke leakage
Listing number
The tested system has an identifier such as a letter code and a number. Read it from the approval sheet, then match the system exactly
Smoke barrier
A wall built to resist smoke, not just flame. Penetrations in it also need sealing
Mechanical systems
Manufactured, presized elastomeric components (modules, blocks, grommets) held in place by mechanical compression, sometimes in a frame. Durable, and they can be reconfigured
Nonmechanical systems
Pliable materials molded or sized to the opening: putties, caulks and sealants, blankets, pads, foams, pillows, and intumescent wraps. Intumescent materials expand with heat; passive ones are endothermic or ablative
Putty pads
Seal the back of an outlet box in a rated wall
Restore the rating
Whatever hole you make, you close with a system that restores the wall's rating
Match the listed system exactly
The wall type, penetrant, opening size, and material must all match the tested system
Label it
Mark the firestop with the system number, the date, and the installer
Inspect it
The AHJ or inspector must accept it before it is covered
Reseal after any change
Adding or removing a cable breaks the seal, so reseal the opening every time
End of the day
A penetration in a fire or smoke barrier is sealed at the end of every workday, not just at the end of the job
Never use
Foam, tape, rags, or insulation as a substitute for a listed system
Not your call
If you cannot find a listed system that fits, stop and ask the designer or the AHJ

Pulling cable 32

Reel stands or boxes
Let the cable unwind without twisting or kinking
Sheaves and rollers
Guide the cable around corners at its bend radius
Pull string or rope
Carries the pulling force, not the cable jacket
Grips and eyes
Attach to the cable with a swivel so the pull does not twist it
Communication
Radios or signals between the pulling end and the feed end
Pull schedule
Lists each cable, its label, its length, and the sequence of the pull
Mark before cutting
Label the cable before you cut it from the reel
Tension, 4-pair cable
110 N (25 lbf) at most, per cable
Bend radius, 4-pair UTP
4 x the cable OD
Bend radius, multipair copper
10 x the cable OD
Bend radius, optical fiber with no load
10 x the cable OD
Bend radius, optical fiber under pulling tension
20 x the cable OD
Manufacturer limits
Win over the numbers above whenever they are stated
Kinks
A kinked cable is damaged. Replace it
Crush
Do not crush a cable with ties, staples, or a tight J-hook; leave bundles loose
Fill
Never exceed the conduit fill limits just to get one more cable in
Lubricant
Only a lubricant listed as compatible with the cable jacket
Top down
Feed from the top with a reel brake at the feed end and support at each floor to take the weight
Bottom up
Use a pull line with a winch, a swivel, and tension monitoring
Cable weight
Heavy backbone cable needs hooks, grips, and supports in proportion; secure it at each floor
Firestop
Every floor opening is firestopped once the cable is in place
Label
Label the cable at every floor; never splice a riser
Work area, 4-pair copper
305 mm (12 in) minimum after termination; not stored in loops
TR or ER, 4-pair
Enough to reach the farthest corner by way of the pathway, plus floor to ceiling
TR or ER, multipair
The length of the backboard plus floor to ceiling
TE
2 m (6.6 ft) stored outside the enclosure
Why
Service slack allows reterminations and moves without a new cable
Where to pull
On the strength member (the aramid yarn or central member), never on the fibers or the jacket
Figure-eight
Lay long runs in a figure eight on the floor to avoid twist, and flip it as you feed
Innerduct
Pull fiber inside an innerduct in conduit and trays, and leave the end of the duct labeled
Cleanliness
Cap the ends, keep dirt out, and never drag cable across a dirty floor
Pulling tension
Stay below the maximum on the cable's specification sheet

Termination 36

One standard per job (Detail)
Pick T568A or T568B and use it for every jack, panel, and cord in the system
Straight-through patch cord (Detail)
Same standard at both ends
Pair 1 (Detail)
Pins 4 and 5, blue pair
Pair 2 (Detail)
Pins 1 and 2
Pair 3 (Detail)
Pins 3 and 6
Pair 4 (Detail)
Pins 7 and 8
Split pair (Detail)
Wires from two different pairs land together as a pair; every pin connects, so continuity passes, but crosstalk fails
Tip colors, in order (Colors)
White, red, black, yellow, violet
Ring colors, in order (Colors)
Blue, orange, green, brown, slate
Pair 1 (Colors)
White-blue
Pair 2 (Colors)
White-orange
Pair 5 (Colors)
White-slate
Pair 6 (Colors)
Red-blue
Pair 25 (Colors)
Violet-slate
Formula for pair n (Colors)
Tip color = group (n - 1) divided by 5, dropping the remainder. Ring color = (n - 1) mod 5
Larger cables (Colors)
Each group of 25 pairs gets its own color-coded binder
110 block
A punch-down block for horizontal and backbone cross-connects. Terminate with a 110 tool; the jacks sit on the connecting block
66 block
An older style punch-down block for voice. A 66 block is for voice only, not for high-speed data
Insulation displacement connector (IDC)
The jaw that cuts through the insulation as you punch the wire down
Patch panel
A rack-mounted panel of jacks; the horizontal cable punches into the back
Jack
Punch each pair to its color code on the jack; keep the pairs twisted as close to the terminals as you can
Strain relief
Tie off or secure the cable so no pull reaches the termination
Connector types
F connector for cable television; BNC for security video
Compression connector
The standard today: clean cut, correct strip, then compress
Strip
Cut the jacket and the center conductor to the length the connector maker shows
Test
Check continuity and look for a shorted center conductor and shield
LC
Small form factor with a latch; the common choice on new work
SC
Square, push-pull connector; common on patch panels
ST
Round bayonet connector with a twist lock; older style
MPO
A multifiber push-on connector that carries many fibers in one ferrule
UPC
Ultra physical contact: a polished end face, blue connector body
APC
Angled physical contact: a polished angled end face, green connector body
Do not mix
Never mate an APC to a UPC; the angled and flat faces damage each other and lose signal
Inspect before you connect
Look at the end face with a scope; if it is dirty, clean it
Cleaning
Dry clean first with a cassette cleaner or swab; use a solvent only if the dry clean fails
Never look
Never look into a fiber end or a connector with a light source on

Testing and troubleshooting 33

Permanent link
The fixed cable and both connectors, without the patch cords. This is what the installer certifies
Channel
The whole path including both patch cords, the connectors, and the cross-connect. This is what the user's equipment sees
Wiremap
Whether each pin connects to the right pin at the far end
Length
The electrical length of each pair; it must stay within the permanent link limit
Insertion loss (IL)
How much signal is lost along the link; lower is better
NEXT
Near-end crosstalk: signal leaking from one pair into another at the end near the tester
PSNEXT
Power sum NEXT: the combined crosstalk from the other three pairs on one pair
FEXT
Far-end crosstalk: signal leaking from one pair into another at the far end of the link
ACR-F
Attenuation-to-crosstalk ratio, far end: how much stronger the signal is than the noise at the far end
Return loss (RL)
Signal reflected back by impedance mismatches, often from a poor termination
Propagation delay
How long the signal takes to travel the link
Delay skew
The difference in delay between the fastest and slowest pair
Open
A wire is not connected or has been cut. Reterminate the pair or find the break
Short
Two wires touch. Check for a stray strand or a staple through the cable
Reversed pair
A pair is wired tip to ring at one end; reterminate that pair
Crossed pair
A pair is on the wrong pins at one end; the jack or the panel was punched in the wrong order
Split pair
One wire from each of two pairs was swapped. The pins connect, but the twist is wrong. Reterminate to the color code
Set the reference
Do this at the start of each session, with the matching adapters
Choose the limit
Pick the permanent link or channel limit for the right category
Choose the cable type
Pick the cable family and the NVP if the tester asks
Autotest
Connect and run the full test
Save with the label
Use the cable label as the name, so the record matches the cable
PASS
Every parameter is within the limit
FAIL
One parameter is outside the limit. Find the cause, fix it, and retest
Marginal asterisk
The result passes, but is within the tester's accuracy of the limit. Treat it as a pass only if the specification allows; many do not
Tester accuracy
Level III covers Category 6 up to 250 MHz; Level IIIe covers Category 6A up to 500 MHz
Cords
Test with the tester's own cords or adapters, and replace them when they wear
Tier 1 test
A light source and a power meter measure total loss in the link. Reference the equipment first, then measure
OLTS
Optical loss test set: a light source and power meter in one box
OTDR
Optical time-domain reflectometer: shows where the loss and reflections are along the fiber. Recognition level
Launch cord
A reference cord used so the first connector is also tested
Clean first
Inspect and clean every connector before testing
Both wavelengths
Test multimode at 850 and 1300 nm and singlemode at 1310 and 1550 nm

Safety, labeling, retrofits, and other systems 25

Site safety plan
Read it on day one and follow it; attend the safety briefing
PPE
Safety glasses, gloves, hard hat, and safety shoes as the site requires; hearing and dust protection when needed
Ladders
Inspect before use, face the ladder, keep three points of contact, and never overreach
Lifts
Be trained before you operate a lift or scaffold; follow the harness rules
Lockout and tagout
Never work on or near energized equipment that has not been locked out and tagged by the person who controls it
Confined spaces
Do not enter a manhole or vault until it is tested, ventilated, and permitted, with a standby person outside
Silica dust
Drilling and coring concrete creates silica dust. Use water or a vacuum and wear a respirator
Asbestos
If you suspect it, stop work, keep others away, and report it. Never disturb or sweep it
Laser safety
Never look into a fiber end; treat every fiber as live until it is proven dark
Lifting
Lift with your legs, ask for help, and carry no more than your limit
First aid
Know where the kit is, who is trained, and how to call for help. Report every injury
Electrical
Treat unknown wires as live; only qualified electricians connect to ac panel grounds
Identifiers
Every space, cable, panel, port, pathway, and bonding conductor gets a unique identifier
Both ends
Label each cable at both ends, and use the same name on both
Where
Within sight of the end, where it can be read without moving the cable
Machine printed
Use a printed, permanent label; never handwriting that smudges
Match the records
The label, the drawing, the panel record, and the tester file must all agree
Records
Keep the administration records, the as-built drawings, and the test results, and hand them over at closeout
Cable tags
Label both ends of a bonding conductor and the sheath of a backbone cable at the rack or ladder rack
PoE type 1
15.4 W
PoE type 2
30 W
PoE type 3
60 W
PoE type 4
90 W
Bundle heating
More power means more heat in a bundle. Use larger-gauge or higher-category cable and smaller bundles for high-power runs
Equipment names
The switch or injector is the power sourcing equipment (PSE); the camera, phone, or access point is the powered device (PD)
